probes.question: Why can the prime p that divides P + 1 not be one of the primes on the list?
options: It would have to divide P + 1 and P, so it would divide 1

probes.question: True or false: Euclid's argument shows that any finite list of primes is missing at least one prime.

image.alt: A torn ancient papyrus fragment of Euclid's Elements with Greek text and a small geometric diagram.

panels.text: Euclid proved in his Elements that there are infinitely many primes. There are now at least 200 proofs, but his was first.
Take any finite list of primes. Multiply them all together to get P, then look at P + 1.
If P + 1 is prime, it is a prime missing from your list. If not, some prime p divides it.
That p cannot be on your list. A listed prime divides P, so it would divide the difference (P + 1) - P = 1, and no prime divides 1. Either way the list was missing a prime.
A myth to drop: it is often told as a proof by contradiction, but Euclid's own argument works by cases.
